source_item.question: An amplitude-loading gate is built from a planar rotation through an angle t(x), where t is any fixed real-valued function of the real parameter x chosen so that on the interval -1 <= x <= 1 the cosine of t(x) equals x (an inverse-cosine branch), and extended in some unspecified way to the rest of the real line. Two claims are on the table: (A) the gate is unitary for every real x, with no restriction and independent of how t is extended; (B) the top-left entry of the gate equals x. Decide for which values of x each claim holds. Prove the unconditional claim, prove that claim (B) holds for -1 <= x <= 1, and prove that claim (B) FAILS whenever |x| > 1 without using any particular value of the extension. Explain the asymmetry: why unitarity is free but the clean-entry readout needs -1 <= x <= 1.
source_item.reference_answer: The gate is the planar rotation with top row (cos t(x), -sin t(x)) and bottom row (sin t(x), cos t(x)). Claim (A) holds unconditionally. For every real angle, cos^2 + sin^2 = 1, so this matrix is a planar rotation and hence unitary (its two entries lie on the unit circle); this is true whatever real number t(x) happens to be, so unitarity holds for all real x and does not depend on how t is extended outside [-1,1]. Claim (B): the top-left entry equals cos t(x). On the interval -1 <= x <= 1 the angle was chosen so that cos t(x) = x, so the top-left entry equals x exactly and the amplitude is loaded correctly. For |x| > 1 the claim fails, and this can be proved without knowing the extension value: the cosine of any real angle lies in the closed interval [-1, 1], so cos t(x) lies in [-1, 1] for every possible choice of t(x); but |x| > 1 means x lies outside [-1, 1], so cos t(x) cannot equal x. Thus the readout is wrong for every |x| > 1 regardless of how t is extended, and no guess about the extension is needed. The asymmetry is the key point: unitarity is a structural property of the rotation shape (two unit-circle entries for any angle), so it survives even a meaningless input; but the clean-entry readout is a semantic promise that the stored amplitude is exactly x, and a cosine can only ever equal numbers in [-1, 1]. A construction can therefore be perfectly unitary yet load the wrong number: a unitarity certificate must not be mistaken for a certificate that the intended coefficient was loaded.

Use column-vector operator convention. The written product W=P_lift† S_lift A_lift P_lift acts chronologically as PREPARE, AMPLITUDE, SELECT, then PREPARE†. It does not apply the leftmost dagger first. All factors act on the same C×(S×H) register, so the products are typed; no clean input or postselection premise is needed for the GLOBAL unitarity proof.

(1) P_lift=I_C tensor(P tensor I_H) is unitary because tensor products of unitary matrices are unitary, and the two identities and selector P are unitary. (2) P_lift† is unitary by adjoint closure of the unitary group. (3) A_lift is block diagonal over contexts (s,x), with coefficient block R_{s,x}; its adjoint product is block diagonal with blocks R_{s,x}†R_{s,x}=I_C, so it is unitary. S_lift is a basis-permutation matrix: each basis column is sent bijectively to |c,s,p_s(x)>, so its columns are orthonormal and it is unitary. (4) Closure under multiplication on the fixed total register now makes W a product of four unitaries. Explicitly,
W†W=P_lift† A_lift† S_lift† P_lift P_lift† S_lift A_lift P_lift
=P_lift† A_lift† A_lift P_lift=I;
the intervening cancellations use P_lift P_lift†=I, S_lift†S_lift=I and A_lift†A_lift=I. The reverse product is I as well. This argument is valid also for empty finite index sets; auxiliary clean labels are used only where they actually exist for a projected block or the examples below.

(5) P† is the defined, sufficient adjoint/inverse choice, but global unitarity does NOT force that choice. Replacing the final selector factor by ANY unitary Q gives Q_lift S_lift A_lift P_lift, again unitary by the same product rule. In particular Q=I uses the known unitary identity and no additional unknown certificate; Q=P inherits unitarity from the existing PREPARE certificate. Thus the old claim that a different final gate cannot be guaranteed unitary from those facts is false. Its clean projected block generally changes: take singleton coefficient/system registers, P=H on a qubit selector, and A=S=I. The chosen W=H†H=I has clean scalar1; the unitary replacement Q=I gives W_Q=H with clean scalar1/sqrt(2). This is a precise distinction between global unitarity and intended LCU clean-entry correctness.

A complete inverse requirement is stronger and does single out the adjoint: if QP=I on the ENTIRE selector space and P is unitary, multiply on the right by P† to get Q=P†. With nontrivial amplitude/SELECT in between, however, the final P† is not adjacent to the original P. Inverting P alone does not invert S_lift A_lift, and global product unitarity says nothing about deterministic auxiliary cleanup.

Preserving only the clean projected block is weaker still. Let clean selector be0, D=diag(1,-1) on a qubit selector, and Q=D P†. Then Q is a distinct unitary with <0|Q=<0|P†. For clean injection J|x>=|c0,0,x>, the full replacement W_Q=D_lift W satisfies J†W_QJ=J†WJ, independently of the particular intervening A,S. This is a shared clean-row LCU subproof with the linked BE004 repair, not a separate new mathematical core. Requiring a particular projected entry/row does not uniquely specify all unitary columns or a full inverse. With singleton coefficient/system and P=I,A=S=I, W=I and W_Q=D already give an explicit distinct pair with the same clean scalar1.

For a direct failure of deterministic cleanup within the CHOSEN architecture itself, take singleton coefficient, selector/system qubits, P=H, amplitude I, and p_0=I,p_1=X for SELECT. On |0,0>, PREPARE then SELECT gives (|0,0>+|1,1>)/sqrt(2). The final P†=H gives (|0,0>+|1,0>+|0,1>-|1,1>)/2 in selector/system notation. Selector1 has probability1/2, despite all three local certificates. The clean projected block is (I+X)/2, not a deterministic normalized system action. In general coefficient leakage can occur too, since its amplitude gates need not fix the chosen clean coefficient label. A deterministic cleanup theorem would require the additional condition (I-JJ†)WJ=0; global unitarity alone does not imply it. This H/controlled-X witness is the same elementary boundary subproof used in the linked BE004 repair; the present core's main task remains assembling global unitarity rather than assigning stage roles.

The source therefore proves a sufficient product-unitarity theorem for its explicit adjoint architecture. It does not prove unique-final-gate necessity or a full-output cleanup property. source_item.reference_answer:
Let c=2^n. Since c>0 and M=2^(n+1)=2c, we have0<=c<M, so c is a genuine index in the specified register. In little-endian bits its only nonzero bit is bit_n; the proof then uses its actual natural integer value c. Substituting into the stated grid gives p_c=-pi L+2^n*(2 pi L/2^(n+1))=-pi L+pi L=0. This identity is independent of the function's signs and of k. For n=0 the register has M=2 points and c=1, so the same calculation holds on one qubit; this is not a claim about a zero-qubit single-point grid.

At that physical point the source middle branch applies. Its zeroth right endpoint jet is S_k(0)=(-1)^0=1, hence f_k(0)=1 and a_c=1. This endpoint identity and the explicit grid-index identity are the TWO facts that realize an actual unit sample. The source lemma smoothInitial_zero derives that value from sourceInterpolant_right_jet at order0; it is not deduced from positivity.

Every real square is nonnegative, regardless of the amplitude's sign. Therefore N=a_c^2+sum_{j!=c}a_j^2=1+sum_{j!=c}a_j^2>=1. In particular N>0 and sqrt(N)>=1>0, so this normalizer is well defined and nonzero. The inference uses only one unit sample and nonnegative squares; it never calls strict positivity of the other amplitudes. Width/order/scale uniformity comes from the same central point and endpoint value persisting for all stipulated k,n,L.

source_item.question: To locate where the left exponential tail meets the polynomial bridge on a grid of 2^n cells, one performs an exact-comparison binary search carrying real interval endpoints: starting from the real interval [lower, lower+span] with span equal to the full width, each of n steps halves the span, forms the midpoint, compares it against the threshold -1, and recurses into the half that still contains the crossing. The search returns an index 'cutIndex'. Prove that this search returns exactly the true cutoff index for every width n and scale L > 0, including the boundary cases where the crossing is at the very first grid point or at the very last, and the single-cell (n = 0) base case. State the exact number of real comparisons and real field operations the search performs.
source_item.reference_answer: Model the search by an interval invariant: at a node with 'remaining' halvings left, 'start' already-decided low-order index, and current interval first point gridPoint(start) and width span = step * 2^remaining, assume the true cutoff c = cutIndex satisfies start <= c <= start + 2^remaining (it lies in the current interval). We prove the returned value equals c by induction on 'remaining'. Base case (remaining = 0, one cell): the interval has a single cell starting at 'start'. The search compares the grid point at 'start' against -1. If gridPoint(start) < -1, then 'start' is still below the threshold, so the crossing is at start+1 and the hypotheses force c = start+1; the search returns start+1. Otherwise 'start' is at or past the threshold, so c = start and the search returns start. In both branches the returned value equals c; this also covers the endpoint boundary cases (crossing at the first or last point) because the invariant pins c to one of the two interval ends when the cell is minimal. Inductive step (remaining+1): the search forms the midpoint, which equals gridPoint(start + 2^remaining) (the first point of the upper half), and compares it to -1. If it is below -1, the crossing lies in the upper half, so recurse with start' = start + 2^remaining and the same remaining; the lower bound updates to start' <= c (since the midpoint is still below threshold, c >= start + 2^remaining) and the width halves, preserving the invariant, so by induction the recursion returns c. If it is at or past -1, the crossing lies in the lower half; recurse with the same start and halved width, and the invariant's upper bound tightens to c <= start + 2^remaining, again returning c. The key geometric identities are span/2 = step * 2^remaining and gridPoint(start) + step*2^remaining = gridPoint(start+2^remaining), which make the carried real endpoints exact — no ceiling evaluation or grid enumeration occurs. Starting the top-level search with the full interval [-pi L, 0] and remaining = n satisfies the initial invariant (the cutoff lies between index 0 and the midpoint index 2^n), so the top-level call returns cutIndex exactly. Cost: each of the n internal halvings performs 2 real field operations (one division to halve the span, one addition to form the midpoint) and 1 real comparison; the base level performs 1 comparison. The top-level producer additionally does one multiplication (pi*L) and one subtraction (0 - width) to initialise the interval. Hence the search proper uses exactly 2n field operations and n+1 comparisons; including initialisation the producer uses 2n+2 field operations and n+1 comparisons. Natural-index arithmetic, powers of two, and counter bookkeeping are outside this real-arithmetic cost model; finite-bit comparison of arbitrary real inputs is not claimed.
